decisions.choice: a bare list of names: each man the father of the next
decisions.reason: Verses 1-4 have no verbs and no words for "son" or "fathered". They give only the names of Genesis 5:3-32, from Adam to Noah, without the ages. Readers who knew Genesis would hear each name as the father of the one after it. The book opens its history of Israel with the first man.

decisions.choice: names joined by commas, one running list through verse 4
alternatives: Adam was the father of Seth, and Seth was the father of Enosh
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the list as the Hebrew gives it, without adding "was the father of", so the bare form of the opening can be seen.

decisions.reason: Up to Noah each name follows the one before it, father to son. The last three names are brothers, the sons of Noah (Genesis 5:32; 10:1); the "and" before Japheth closes the group. The next verses take up each brother's line, Japheth first.

This verse is Genesis 10:2. Many of the names are peoples: Madai is the Medes, Javan the Ionian Greeks.

decisions.choice: the list formula of the genealogies
decisions.reason: Literal keeps each "and" of the Hebrew; Balanced keeps the list with a colon; Readable says "X's sons were". The same wording is used through the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 1-9.

The words may have dropped out in copying, or Chronicles counts Aram's sons as Shem's descendants ("sons" can mean descendants). Either way the four are Shem's line through Aram.

decisions.choice: Meshech: Mash in Genesis 10:23

decisions.choice: Peleg ... was divided: a play on the name

decisions.choice: the earth was divided: most likely the scattering at Babel
decisions.reason: "The earth" can mean its people (Genesis 11:1). The division is most likely the dividing of humankind into peoples and languages (Genesis 11:8-9). Others take it as a division of land.

decisions.choice: which means "division"; the people of the earth
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name so the reason given makes sense (m1), and says "the people of" the earth (m2), as Genesis 10:25 does.

decisions.reason: Genesis 25:1 says Abraham "took a wife" named Keturah, and Genesis 25:6 speaks of the sons of his concubines. A concubine (pilegesh) was a true wife of lower rank, whose sons did not share the main inheritance; Chronicles gives Keturah that title.

decisions.choice: concubine (a secondary wife)

decisions.choice: daughter of Mezahab: descendant of Mezahab
decisions.reason: "Daughter" here means descendant, as in Genesis 36:39. Mezahab ("waters of gold") may be a person or a place.

decisions.choice: granddaughter of Mezahab
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say granddaughter, as Genesis 36:39 does (m2).

decisions.choice: Hadad's death, then the chiefs of Genesis 36:40-43

decisions.reason: Genesis 36:39 does not record the death of the last king, perhaps because he was still reigning when that list was made; Chronicles adds it. The list of chiefs that follows is Genesis 36:40-43, the heads of Edom's clans and districts, without its opening "by their clans, by their places". The "and" joins the two lists; it need not mean that chiefs replaced the kings.

decisions.choice: Alvah, as the text is read
decisions.reason: The Hebrew letters spell Aliah, but the vowels and the scribes' note read Alvah, the name in Genesis 36:40.

decisions.choice: "chief" said once at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: Literal repeats "chief" before each name as the Hebrew does; Balanced and Readable say it once, as Genesis 36:40 does. Readable says "leaders of the family groups", as there.
